bib.title: Voicebox: Text-Guided Multilingual Universal Speech Generation at Scale

question: Can a single non-autoregressive speech model trained at scale on text-guided infilling perform many speech generation tasks in-context, and beat task-specific SOTA?
hypothesis: Scale plus a flexible infilling objective with flow matching lets speech models generalise to unseen tasks like LLMs do.
contributions: Voicebox learns text-guided speech infilling at scale and solves tasks it was not explicitly trained on via in-context learning.
Voicebox outperforms VALL-E with new SOTA English zero-shot TTS (5.9%->1.9% WER, 0.580->0.681 similarity).
First model with high-quality cross-lingual zero-shot TTS across six languages without style labels, pretrained embedders or multilingual samples.
Infills speech of any length and outperforms A3T on text-guided denoising.
Generates diverse realistic speech: ASR trained solely on synthetic speech loses only 0.4%/1.7% absolute WER.

method.summary: Voicebox is a non-autoregressive continuous normalizing flow trained with flow matching (OT path) to infill masked 80-d Mel frames given the surrounding audio and a frame-level phone transcript, plus a separate duration model (regression or flow matching). Tasks (zero-shot TTS, denoising, editing, style transfer, diverse sampling) are cast as different context masks at inference; classifier-free guidance and ODE step count trade quality for speed.

datasets.name: English audiobooks (ASR-transcribed)
datasets.source: audiobooks, ASR-transcribed; named only as 'English audiobooks'
datasets.preprocessing: MFA phonemisation and forced alignment; 80-d log Mel at 100 Hz, normalised mean -5.884 std 2.261

datasets.name: Multilingual audiobooks (En, Fr, De, Es, Pl, Pt)
LibriSpeech test-clean (filtered, 4-10 s)
datasets.preprocessing: 3 s prompt: another sample of same speaker (cross-sentence) or first 3 s (continuation)

datasets.name: MLS test splits (filtered)
datasets.size: 3535 En, 2323 Es, 3183 De, 2284 Fr, 508 Pl, 838 Pt after filtering
datasets.preprocessing: kept Whisper-transcript WER <20% (<30% Pl, Pt) and MFA alignment success

datasets.name: LibriSpeech test-other text / train text
datasets.split: test-other text (diverse sampling); train text (ASR data)

datasets.name: 1K-hour English audiobook subset
datasets.source: subset used for ablations and FSD reference

models.name: Voicebox audio model (VB-En / VB-Multi)
models.architecture: Transformer with conv positional embedding, symmetric bi-directional ALiBi, UNet-style skip connections; flow-matching CNF
models.tokenizer: MFA phones with word-position postfixes and ghost silence

other.input: 80-d log Mel at 100 Hz; flow step as sinusoidal embedding prepended

models.name: Voicebox duration model
models.architecture: Transformer, regression (L1) or conditional flow matching
models.hidden: 512 En / 768 Multi per Table D14 (text says 512/2048 for both)

models.name: VALL-E
models.architecture: AR + NAR codec LM on Encodec

other.note: model not available; numbers from its paper

models.name: A3T
models.architecture: NAR regression infilling model trained on VCTK

models.name: RNN-T Conformer ASR
models.architecture: 20-layer conformer encoder 512-d, 8 heads, FFN 2048; LSTM predictor 512-d; 4096 wordpieces

other.training: Adam, 120 epochs, tri-stage lr max 0.001 (0.0001 for 100h), clip 10, weight decay 0.1, SpecAugment; beam 15

training.objective: Masked conditional flow matching (OT path, sigma_min) on infilling: L=E||m*(u_t(x_t|x)-v_t(x_t,x_ctx,z;theta))||^2; duration: masked CFM or masked L1 regression
training.lr_schedule: linear warmup then linear decay over rest of training
training.seq_len: audio capped at 1,600 frames, random chunking
training.hardware: 32 GPUs audio, 4 GPUs duration, 8 GPUs vocoder (GPU type not stated)
training.compute: vocoder 7.5 days on 8 GPUs; audio model wall-clock not stated

other.masking: with pdrop 0.3/0.2 (audio/duration) whole sequence masked, otherwise contiguous segment of r% with r~U[70,100] audio / U[10,100] duration
other.cfg: alpha chosen empirically per task; 0.7 for En TTS and denoising, 1.0 for multilingual

inference.decoding: ODE solve (torchdiffeq), midpoint solver, step size 0.0625 (NFE=32) by default; regression duration model by default; silence at both ends trimmed to 0.1 s max
inference.samples: one sample per item; FM duration model averaged over 20 samples only for duration metrics; no seeds stated
inference.prompting: 3 s audio prompt + its transcript concatenated with target text

parameters.cfg_alpha: 0.7 English TTS and denoising, 1.0 multilingual, 0 for diverse sampling
parameters.cfg_formula: v~ = (1+alpha) v(w,x_ctx,z) - alpha v(w); each evaluation costs two forward passes

metrics.name: WER
metrics.definition: ASR transcription of output vs input text; HuBERT-L (English) or Whisper large-v2 (multilingual)

metrics.name: SIM-o
metrics.definition: WavLM-TDCNN speaker embedding cosine similarity to original audio context

metrics.name: FSD
metrics.definition: Frechet distance on wav2vec 2.0 BASE layer-6 features, real vs generated

metrics.name: QMOS/SMOS
metrics.definition: crowd MOS via CrowdMOS, 50 samples x 10 ratings, 95% CI

eval.protocol: Single run per configuration, no seeds or significance tests stated; MOS with 95% CI.

availability.data: audio samples at voicebox.metademolab.com; training data unnamed audiobooks

evidence.quote: 512/2048 embedding/FFN dimensions, with 8/10 layers for English/multilingual
evidence.where: Sec 5.1 text says 512 for both; Table D14 gives 512 En and 768 Multi

results.claim: Voicebox beats VALL-E on zero-shot TTS word error rate (cross-sentence prompt).
results.setup: VB-En, filtered LibriSpeech test-clean (4-10 s), 3 s cross-sentence prompt, midpoint solver NFE=32, WER from HuBERT-L ASR; VALL-E number as reported in its paper.
results.table: Table 2, cross-sentence, rows VB-En (1.9) and VALL-E (5.9), column WER

results.claim: Voicebox speaker similarity to the (resynthesised) audio context exceeds VALL-E's.
results.setup: Same as above; SIM-r uses WavLM-TDCNN against vocoder-resynthesised context.
results.table: Table 2, cross-sentence, rows VB-En (0.681) and VALL-E (0.580), column SIM-r

results.claim: Against raw (original) context, Voicebox SIM-o is 0.662 cross-sentence; on continuation the gap over VALL-E is +0.141 SIM-o.
results.setup: LS test-clean, 3 s prompt; VALL-E continuation SIM-o obtained from authors by communication.
results.note: Table 2 continuation: VB-En (alpha=0.7) SIM-o 0.593 vs VALL-E 0.452 (asterisk, from authors).
results.quote: the gap is even bigger when compared against raw audio (+0.141 SIM-o on continuation)

results.claim: Voicebox is about 20x faster than VALL-E at low NFE without guidance.
results.setup: Inference time for 10 s of audio incl. vocoding and duration prediction, NFE=2, no CFG; VALL-E is the authors' re-implementation (6.2 s vs 10 s in original).
results.quote: For NFE=2 without CFG, Voicebox takes about 0.31 seconds, about 20 times faster than VALL-E.

results.claim: At NFE=64 Voicebox is only slightly slower than VALL-E, so the speed advantage is a function of NFE.
results.setup: Same timing setup, NFE=64.
results.quote: At NFE=64, Voicebox is only 4% slower than VALL-E.

results.claim: Cross-lingual zero-shot TTS: Voicebox cuts average English-target WER vs YourTTS and raises similarity.
results.setup: VB-Multi (alpha=1.0), filtered MLS test sets, 3 s context from each of 6 languages (36 directions); WER from Whisper large-v2. Averages from contribution list.
results.quote: Compared to the prior cross-lingual SOTA YourTTS, Voicebox reduces the average WER from 10.9% to 5.2%, and improves audio similarity from 0.335 to 0.481.

results.claim: On En/Fr/Pt (YourTTS-supported) Voicebox has lower WER and higher SIM-o than YourTTS, averaged over six context languages.
results.setup: MLS, same setup.
results.quote: Voicebox obtains 3.1%/5.9%/8.1% lower WERs and 0.136/0.141/0.160 higher similarity averaged across audio context in six languages.

results.claim: Subjective similarity and quality also favour Voicebox in cross-lingual TTS.
results.setup: MLS English target text, prompts in 6 languages, 50 samples x 10 ratings, 95% CI.
results.quote: The average audio similarity MOS is 0.59 (3.89 vs 3.30) higher for Voicebox and the average quality MOS is 0.27 (3.50 vs. 3.23) higher.

results.claim: Transient noise removal: Voicebox infilling reaches near-clean WER where Demucs does not.
results.setup: Librispeech test-clean mixed with non-speech noise over 50% of duration at -10 dB SNR; A3T and Voicebox given transcript and noise location, Demucs not.
results.table: Table 5, row VB-En (alpha = 0.7), column WER (2.0); Demucs 32.5, A3T 11.5, noisy 41.2

results.claim: Voicebox denoising quality MOS vs baselines.
results.setup: Same noise setup; QMOS 1-5, 95% CI.
results.table: Table 5, row VB-En (alpha = 0.7), column QMOS (3.87); Demucs 2.86, A3T 3.10

results.claim: A synthetic-only ASR training set from Voicebox is within 0.4/1.7 absolute WER of real data.
results.setup: RNN-T Conformer ASR trained on 281K synthetic utterances (one per LibriSpeech train text), VB-En alpha=0, FM duration; vs real 960 h; test-other / test-clean.
results.note: With 4-gram LM, Table 7: 2.6 vs 2.2 on test-clean (0.4) and 6.7 vs 5.0 on test-other (1.7). The contribution list says '0.4%/1.7% ... test-other/test-clean', which is reversed relative to the table. No-LM gaps are 0.5 and 2.0.
results.quote: only lags behind real data by 0.4% and 1.7% absolute

results.claim: ASR trained on Voicebox data with FM duration, no LM, WER on test-other.
results.setup: Table 7, trained on synthetic only, tested on real LS.
results.note: baseline_value is VITS-VCTK no-LM test-other (55.5); YourTTS 54.6; VITS-LJ 81.2.
results.table: Table 7, row VB-En (alpha = 0, dur=FM, alpha_dur = 0), column No LM test-o

results.claim: Voicebox diverse samples have far lower FSD than baselines, even below real test-other audio.
results.setup: LS test-other text, text-only sampling, FSD with wav2vec 2.0 layer 6.
results.table: Table 6, row VB-En (alpha = 0, dur=regr), column FSD (155.7); ground truth 171.1, YourTTS 277.9

results.claim: Flow matching with OT path trains much faster than diffusion-path variants.
results.setup: Reduced setup (1K h data, smaller model, lr 1e-4, loss on all frames), NFE=32, zero-shot TTS; at 50K updates.
results.table: Table 8, row FM w/ OT, upd=50K WER 2.5; FM w/ diff 76.0; SM w/ diff 73.3

results.claim: FM with OT produces good results at 8 NFEs; diffusion variants need 16 or more than 64.
results.setup: Reduced setup, 150K updates.
results.quote: which can produce good results with just 8 NFEs, while FM w/ diff requires at least 16 NFEs and SM w/ diff requires over 64 NFEs

results.claim: A flow-matching audio model beats a regression audio model on similarity and diversity while WER is similar.
results.setup: 1K h English, 12-layer 1024-d model, 150k steps, batch 120k frames; masked loss.
results.table: Table B2, row Flow Matching / Masked, SIM-r 0.597, FSD 242.5; Regression / Masked SIM-r 0.520, FSD 278.8

results.claim: More training data improves zero-shot TTS WER and SIM-r (monotone from 60 h to 60,000 h).
results.setup: Reduced setup, cross-sentence; subsets 0.1/1/10/100% of 60K h English.
results.note: FSD got worse from 6K h to 60K h (195.52 to 214.38); authors attribute to a 1K-hour reference distribution.
results.table: Table B3, rows 60 (WER 2.30, SIM-r 0.151) and 60,000 (WER 2.05, SIM-r 0.645)

results.claim: Prompt length: SIM-r grows with longer prompts and Voicebox matches VALL-E's similarity with about two thirds of the audio.
results.setup: Zero-shot TTS 5.2, regression duration, alpha 0.7, NFE 32; read from Fig 6.
results.quote: achieving the same speaker similarity as VALL-E with roughly two thirds the input audio

results.claim: Cross-lingual WER rises with prompt length for most directions, worst from English to non-English.
results.setup: MLS, targets truncated to 4 s; authors blame English being over 90% of multilingual data.
results.quote: English accounts for over 90% of the multilingual training data

results.claim: Original vs Voicebox-generated speech is trivially detectable by a CNN classifier; resynthesised vs generated is harder at low mask rates.
results.setup: Classifier trained on 100 h subset, tested on LS dev-clean-sized split, alpha 0.7, NFE 64.
results.table: Table 10, rows Resynthesized vs Voicebox-generated: 30% mask accuracy 0.704, 50% 0.809, 90% 0.907

results.claim: Audio-model skip connections and ALiBi: authors report ALiBi helps convergence and extrapolation (no number).
results.setup: Appendix A.6.
results.quote: we find ALiBi Bias to improve convergence and extrapolation to longer sequences

limits: Preprint, under review: venue stated as 'Preprint. Under review.' in the PDF; NeurIPS 2023 is not confirmed by the text.
Trained on read audiobook speech in up to six languages; may not transfer to conversational speech with laughter or backchannels.
Depends on a phonemizer and forced aligner; word-based phonemizers miss context-dependent pronunciation (e.g. French liaison).
No independent control of voice versus emotion or other attributes.
VALL-E was not available; its numbers are copied from its paper, and the latency comparison uses the authors' re-implementation.
Training data, code and weights are not released in the paper; GPU type and wall-clock for the audio model are not stated.
Lower WER does not imply better quality; regression duration lowers WER partly by being more regular.
Performance of English-prompt cross-lingual TTS degrades with longer prompts due to English-dominated data.
